headline: Support Group for People Who Waved at Someone Not Waving at Them Holds First In-Person Meetup
subheadline: Members debate whether to wave at each other or maintain ironic distance
summary: An online community dedicated to the specific shame of misdirected waves gathered in person for the first time.
content:
The Threadit community r/WavedAtNoOne held its first in-person meetup last Saturday, bringing together 847 members who share a common trauma: waving enthusiastically at someone who was waving at the person behind them.

"I saw someone waving across a parking lot," recalled organizer @FriendlyToAFault. "Full arm, big smile. I waved back. They were waving at their mom. Their mom saw me wave. I still think about it."

The meetup, held at a community center, began awkwardly when members struggled with the fundamental question of whether to greet each other with waves. "We stood in a circle for like five minutes," said attendee @ArmWentUp. "Nobody wanted to wave first because what if someone wasn't waving back? What if this was all an elaborate trap?"

Eventually, they established a protocol: all waves must be preceded by direct eye contact and verbal confirmation of intent to wave. The system worked, though several members described it as "emotionally exhausting."

The community was founded in 2022 after @FriendlyToAFault posted about converting a mistaken wave into a hair adjustment—a move the community has since termed "the pivot." The post went viral, generating 15,000 comments from fellow sufferers sharing their own recovery techniques.

Popular strategies discussed at the meetup included the "phone check" (pretending you were reaching for your phone), the "full commit" (waving harder to assert dominance over the situation), and the "embrace the chaos" school which advocates waving at everyone regardless of intent.

"I've waved at 847 strangers this year," said @WaveWarrior. "Most don't wave back. I don't care anymore. I've been freed by exposure therapy."

The meetup concluded with a "wave circle" where members practiced waving at each other with no ambiguity. Several participants reported crying. "It was the first time I waved and knew—knew—it was reciprocated," said @HealingOneWaveAtATime. "Transformative."
author: Jennifer Park, Human Interest Reporter
